questions.question: What is Git and why is it called a distributed version control system?
questions.title: What Is Git?
questions.direct_answer: Git is a distributed version control system where every developer has a full copy of the entire project history on their local machine, unlike centralized systems that rely on a single server.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the fundamentals of source control and can articulate what 'distributed' means in practice
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Git with GitHub — Git is the tool, GitHub is just a hosting service for Git repositories
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the offline capability and the speed advantage of local operations

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: So Git is a distributed version control system. The key word here is distributed — it means every developer has a complete copy of the repository on their own machine, including the entire history of every commit ever made. Compare that to an older centralized system like SVN, where there's one central server and developers only have the latest snapshot locally. With Git, if the server goes down, no one loses their history because everyone has the full history themselves. Another huge benefit is speed — operations like viewing history, creating branches, or even committing are all local and happen instantly, without any network round-trip. Git was created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 to manage the Linux kernel codebase, and it's now the industry standard for version control. When you ask 'what makes Git special,' it comes down to three things: distributed architecture, speed, and its incredibly powerful branching model.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Every developer has a full local copy of the repository and its complete history
Distributed means no single point of failure — work continues even if the remote is down
Local operations (log, diff, branch) are nearly instant because no network call is needed
Git ≠ GitHub — Git is the VCS tool; GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket are hosting platforms
Created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 for the Linux kernel project

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java developer using Git to manage a Spring Boot project with feature branches
speakable_v2.hook: Most developers confuse Git with GitHub — but Git's superpower is that your laptop already holds the entire project history.

beats.content: Git is a distributed version control system — every developer's machine holds a complete copy of the project history, not just the latest files. You don't need the server to view old commits, create branches, or make new ones.

Before Git, teams used centralized tools like SVN where one server held everything. If that server went down, work stopped. Linus Torvalds built Git in 2005 so the Linux kernel team could work offline and at speed.

content: Local repo: the full history lives right on your laptop inside the .git folder
Remote repo: a shared copy (GitHub, GitLab) that the team syncs to
Working directory: where you actually edit files before staging and committing

beats.content: In a Spring Boot project, when you run git log on your laptop, Git doesn't hit GitHub at all — it reads the local .git database. candidates miss: that's why git log and git diff are instant even with thousands of commits in the history.

content: Git is not GitHub — Git is the tool, GitHub is just one hosting service for Git repos
Distributed doesn't mean chaotic — teams still agree on one authoritative remote like GitHub as the source of truth

speakable_v2.cap: Git's distributed model means your full history is always local — fast, offline, and safe from server outages.

questions.question: How does Git differ from SVN (Subversion)?
questions.title: Git vs SVN
questions.direct_answer: Git is a distributed VCS where each developer has the full history locally; SVN is a centralized VCS where history lives only on a central server.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of what distributed vs centralized means and practical trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying Git is 'better' without explaining why — always back it up with specifics
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that SVN has simpler access control which is why some enterprises still use it

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The core difference is centralized versus distributed. In SVN, there's one central server that holds the entire history. Developers check out a working copy, make changes, and commit back to that single server. If the server is unavailable, no one can commit or view history. Git flips this model — every developer clones the full repository, meaning they have every commit, every branch, and the complete history right on their laptop. This enables offline commits, extremely fast branching, and resilience to server outages. In terms of branching, SVN branches are basically just directory copies under a different folder, which is expensive and awkward. Git branches are just lightweight pointers to commits, so creating or switching branches is near-instantaneous. The trade-off is that Git has a steeper learning curve, and fine-grained access control at the directory level is harder with Git than SVN. But for the vast majority of modern software teams, Git's distributed nature and branching model make it the clear choice.

sections.title: Key Points
content: SVN: centralized — one server holds history; Git: distributed — full history on every machine
SVN requires network access to commit; Git commits are local and instant
Git branches are lightweight pointers (cheap to create); SVN branches are directory copies (expensive)
Git enables offline workflows; SVN does not
SVN still used in some enterprises for path-based access control

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java developer using Git to manage a Spring Boot project with feature branches
speakable_v2.hook: SVN and Git both track changes — but their architecture is completely different, and that gap matters daily.

content: SVN (Subversion) is centralized — one server holds the entire history. Developers check out a working copy and must connect to that server to commit, view logs, or create branches. Server down means work stops.
Git is distributed — every developer clones the full repository including all history to their own machine. You commit, branch, and inspect history locally without any network call.
Pick Git for almost any new project — it's the industry standard and enables fast branching workflows
SVN survives in enterprises that need fine-grained path-level access control, which Git doesn't natively support

beats.content: In a Spring Boot project, a developer on a flight can still git commit, git branch, and git log freely. With SVN the same developer would be stuck — every one of those actions needs the central server.

speakable_v2.cap: Git wins on speed, offline capability, and branching — SVN's only remaining edge is path-level access control in large enterprises.

questions.question: What are the three areas (or stages) in Git's local workflow?
questions.title: Git's Three Areas: Working Directory, Staging Area, Repository
questions.direct_answer: Git has three areas: the working directory (where you edit files), the staging area or index (where you prepare the next commit), and the local repository (the committed history stored in .git).

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Git's internal model — this is foundational for understanding add/commit/stash
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking 'commit' goes directly from the working directory — the staging step is often missed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why the staging area is useful — you can commit only a subset of your changes

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Git has three distinct areas you work with locally. First is the working directory — this is just your file system, the folder where you're actually editing code. When you modify a file, those changes exist only here initially. Second is the staging area, also called the index. This is a preparatory zone where you move changes you want to include in your next commit using 'git add'. Think of it like a package you're assembling before shipping. Third is the local repository — this is the .git folder inside your project. When you run 'git commit', Git takes everything in the staging area and creates a permanent snapshot in this repository. The reason the staging area is useful is that you might have modified five files, but you only want to commit changes to two of them right now. You selectively 'git add' those two files, commit them as a logical unit, and the other three remain in your working directory for a later commit. This lets you craft clean, focused commits rather than one giant messy commit.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Working Directory: your actual files on disk — changes here are 'unstaged'
Staging Area (Index): a draft of your next commit — populated by 'git add'
Local Repository (.git): the committed history — written to by 'git commit'
Flow: edit file → git add (stage) → git commit (save to repo)
The staging area enables selective commits — you control exactly what goes into each commit

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java developer using Git to manage a Spring Boot project with feature branches
speakable_v2.hook: Most beginners skip straight from editing to committing — but there's a crucial middle step that gives you control over exactly what goes into each commit.

beats.content: Git's local workflow has three areas: the working directory where you edit code, the staging area (also called the index) where you prepare your next commit, and the local repository (the .git folder) where committed history lives permanently.

The staging area exists so you can be deliberate about what goes into each commit. You might touch five files, but only three of them belong to the same logical change — stage just those three and commit them cleanly.

content: Working directory: files on disk, changes are 'unstaged' until you run git add
Staging area (index): a draft snapshot assembled with git add — what the next commit will contain
Local repository (.git folder): permanent committed history written by git commit

beats.content: In a Spring Boot project you edit UserService.java and application.properties. You only want to commit the service change right now. Run git add UserService.java, then git commit. non-obvious: application.properties stays in the working directory untouched — it's not staged so it won't sneak into that commit.

content: Running git add . stages everything including .env or config files you never meant to commit — be selective
Skipping git status before committing means you can't see what's staged vs unstaged

speakable_v2.cap: Think of staging as assembling a package before shipping — you decide exactly what goes in before sealing it with git commit.

questions.question: Is a Git commit a diff (set of changes) or a snapshot of the entire project?
questions.title: Git Commits Are Snapshots, Not Diffs
questions.direct_answer: A Git commit is a snapshot of all tracked files at that point in time, not a diff — though Git is smart about storing only changed content to save space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of understanding of Git internals — separates candidates who've truly learned Git from those who've just used it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying a commit stores only the changes — this is how SVN works, not Git
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Git uses SHA-1 content addressing and stores blob objects for file contents

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: This is a common misconception. Git commits are snapshots, not diffs. When you commit, Git saves a complete picture of what every tracked file looks like at that exact moment. Compare this to SVN, which stores a base version and then a series of deltas or differences. Git's model might sound inefficient — does it copy every file on every commit? Not quite. Git is clever: if a file hasn't changed between two commits, Git doesn't store it again, it simply reuses a reference to the existing stored object. Under the hood, each file is stored as a 'blob' object with a SHA-1 hash, and if the content is identical, the same blob is referenced. So you get the conceptual simplicity of snapshots — every commit is self-contained and you can reconstruct any version instantly — with storage efficiency. This is why Git is so fast at switching branches or checking out old commits: it's not replaying diffs, it's just pointing to a snapshot.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Git commits are snapshots of the full project state, not incremental diffs
SVN stores deltas (diffs); Git stores snapshots — this is a fundamental architectural difference
Git optimizes storage: unchanged files are referenced (not copied) using content-addressable SHA-1 hashes
Snapshots make branch switching and history navigation very fast
Each commit also stores metadata: author, timestamp, commit message, and parent commit hash

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java developer using Git to manage a Spring Boot project with feature branches
speakable_v2.hook: Interviewers love this one — most people think a commit is just 'what changed', but Git's model is fundamentally different.

beats.content: A Git commit is a snapshot — it captures the complete state of every tracked file at that exact moment. It's not a diff. Every commit is a full, self-contained picture of the project.
Snapshots make operations like branch switching and checkout blazing fast. Git doesn't have to replay a chain of diffs — it just points to the right snapshot and you're done.

content: Blob objects: each file's content stored by SHA-1 hash — identical content reuses the same blob
Tree objects: represent directory structure pointing to blobs
Commit object: metadata (author, message, timestamp) plus a pointer to the root tree

beats.content: In a Spring Boot project with 200 files, if you change only UserService.java and commit, Git stores one new blob for that file and reuses 199 existing blobs for the rest. sharp edge: the storage cost is tiny, but the conceptual model is always 'full snapshot' — that's what makes git checkout so fast.

content: Saying 'Git stores diffs' is wrong — that's SVN's model; confusing them in an interview is a red flag
Snapshots don't mean Git wastes disk — SHA-1 deduplication means unchanged files cost almost nothing

speakable_v2.cap: Every Git commit is a complete snapshot, not a patch — that's why branch switching and history are instant.

questions.question: What is the difference between git init and git clone?
questions.title: git init vs git clone
questions.direct_answer: 'git init' creates a brand new empty repository in the current folder; 'git clone' copies an existing remote repository (including all history) to your local machine.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Git command knowledge and when to use each
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using git init on a project that already exists on GitHub instead of git clone
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that git clone also sets up the 'origin' remote automatically and configures tracking branches

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: These two commands serve completely different purposes. 'git init' is for starting fresh — you run it in an empty folder, or an existing project folder that isn't yet under version control, and it creates a new .git directory there. At this point, the repository has no commits and no remote configured. You'd use this when you're creating a brand-new project from scratch. 'git clone', on the other hand, is for joining an existing project. It downloads the entire repository — every commit, every branch, every tag — from a remote URL to a new folder on your machine. It also automatically configures the remote as 'origin' and sets up tracking so that your local main branch tracks origin/main. In practice, as a new developer joining a team, you'll use 'git clone' far more often than 'git init'. You'd use 'git init' when you're starting a new side project locally and then pushing it up to GitHub for the first time.

sections.title: Key Points
content: git init: creates a new empty repository locally; no history, no remote configured
git clone <url>: copies an existing repository including full history to your machine
git clone auto-configures 'origin' as the remote and sets up branch tracking
Use git init for new projects; use git clone to join an existing project
After git init, you typically add a remote with: git remote add origin <url>

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java developer using Git to manage a Spring Boot project with feature branches
speakable_v2.hook: New developers mix these up constantly — one starts a brand-new repo, the other joins an existing one.

content: git init creates an empty Git repository in the current folder. It makes a .git directory with no commits, no history, and no remote configured. Use it when you're starting a project from scratch on your machine.

git clone copies an existing remote repository — every commit, branch, and tag — to a new local folder. It also auto-configures origin as the remote and sets up tracking so plain git push and git pull just work.
Use git init when you're creating a new project locally that doesn't exist on GitHub yet
Use git clone whenever you're joining a team project or downloading an open-source repo

beats.content: Starting a new Spring Boot project on your laptop? git init. Joining a team's existing Spring Boot repo on GitHub? git clone https://github.com/team/spring-app.git — and you're ready to work.

speakable_v2.cap: git init is for starting fresh; git clone is for joining an existing project — use clone far more often in team settings.
